Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

- Working diagnosis (supported by transcript): Acute diarrheal illness (acute gastroenteritis) likely.

- Key differential diagnoses (from DDx, consistent with transcript):
  - Acute viral gastroenteritis: High likelihood; onset ~3 days, 4–5 loose stools/day, watery stool, occasional abdominal pain, no blood, patient able to maintain hydration.
  - Acute bacterial gastroenteritis: Medium likelihood; similar presentation but less clear exposure/fever; possible but less supported by history.
  - SSRI-induced diarrhea (Lexapro): Medium likelihood; Lexapro use can cause GI upset; temporal relationship not explicitly defined in transcript.
  - Inflammatory bowel disease flare: Low–Medium likelihood; possible but less likely given acute 3-day course and absence of hematochezia or chronic history.

- Plan and management (from transcript):
  - Hydration: Emphasize continuing oral fluids; watch for signs of dehydration; seek care if diarrhea occurs 6–8 times per day or if dehydration develops.
  - Diet: Implement soft diet (crackers, toast, jam, easily digested foods). Avoid dairy, fish, meat, and eggs while diarrheal symptoms persist. Progress to boiled vegetables and mashed foods after 48 hours of symptom improvement; reintroduce meat gradually.
  - Probiotics: Yogurt recommended as a probiotic source to support gut flora.
  - Antidiarrheal/replacement: Consider OTC Dioralyte or similar oral rehydration solution to replenish lost salts.
  - When to test/treat further: If diarrhea persists beyond one week, or if there is blood in stool, obtain a stool sample to evaluate for infectious etiologies and possible need for antibiotics.
  - Dehydration warning: If stool frequency reaches 6–8 times per day, consider hospital assessment for dehydration.
  - Documentation: All information provided and instructions will be recorded in the patient-app notes for review.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Acute viral gastroenteritis (High): Most consistent with acute onset, 4–5 watery stools/day, abdominal pain, mild or no fever, no blood, and preserved hydration.
- Acute bacterial gastroenteritis (Medium): Plausible given diarrhea and abdominal pain but less supported due to lack of travel/exposure history and no systemic toxicity.
- SSRI-induced diarrhea (Medium): Possible contributor due to Lexapro use; temporal relationship not defined.
- Inflammatory bowel disease (Low): Possible but unlikely given acute 3-day history and lack of hematochezia or chronic symptoms.
- Ischemic/vascular GI etiologies (Low): Not suggested by history but considered in DDx; no typical risk factors or presentation.

- Likelihood and justification:
  - Acute viral gastroenteritis — High: Onset, stool characteristics, absence of blood, hydration status, and overall clinical picture align with a common self-limited infectious enteritis.
  - Acute bacterial gastroenteritis — Medium: Similar symptoms; exposure history not identified; absence of fever or systemic toxicity lowers likelihood.
  - SSRI-induced diarrhea — Medium: Medication list includes Lexapro; GI side effects are known; requires temporal correlation not documented.
  - Inflammatory bowel disease — Low: Acute, self-resolving course without chronic symptoms or bleeding.
  - Ischemic GI — Low: No vascular risk factors or concerning features.

- Transcript quality notes: Clear overall; minor potential confusion around Lexapro vs inhaler naming encountered in the dialogue; no audio quality issues noted.
